question: Can you list for me all the usa secretaries of education from the beginning of 2018 until the end of 2024? including short acting secretaries
response:
USA Secretaries of Education (including acting), **from the beginning of 2018 through the end of 2024**:

- **Betsy DeVos** — Secretary of Education — **Feb 7, 2017 – Jan 8, 2021**
- **Mick Zais** — *Acting* Secretary of Education — **Jan 8, 2021 – Jan 20, 2021**
- **Phil Rosenfelt** — *Acting* Secretary of Education — **Jan 20, 2021 – Mar 2, 2021**
- **Miguel Cardona** — Secretary of Education — **Mar 2, 2021 – Jan 20, 2025** (so he served through all of **2024**)

Source: Wikipedia, “United States Secretary of Education” (table of officeholders/acting officeholders): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education

# At a Glance: U.S. Secretaries of Education

The U.S. Department of Education has had 13 secretaries since its birth as a Cabinet-level department in 1980. Some have served for an entire presidential administration, others for less than a year. They’ve used their perch at the helm of the Education Department to push a broad basket of policy priorities, from standardized testing and broader civil rights enforcement to a rollback of the federal footprint in K-12. And they’ve come from a range of backgrounds, including that of former governor, federal judiciary, state schools chief, big-city superintendent, and outspoken policy advocate.

The **United States secretary of education** is the head of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the president of the United States, and the federal government, on policies, programs, and activities related to all education in the United States. As a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), the secretary is sixteenth in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-2) Prior to its creation as an Executive Department, there was a non-Cabinet level position called the [United States commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commissioner_of_Education "United States Commissioner of Education") who led the [United States Office of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Education "United States Office of Education").

The current secretary of education is [Linda McMahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon"), serving in this role under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-3)

## Function

The United States secretary of education is a member of the [president's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and is the sixteenth in the [United States presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-4) This secretary deals with federal influence over [education policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy "Education policy"), and heads the United States Department of Education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-5)

The secretary is advised by the [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACIQI "NACIQI"), an advisory committee, on "matters related to accreditation and to the eligibility and certification process for institutions of higher education."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-6)

## List of secretaries

Prior to the creation of the Department of Education in 1979, Education was a division of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.

# At a Glance: U.S. Secretaries of Education

The U.S. Department of Education has had 13 secretaries since its birth as a Cabinet-level department in 1980. Some have served for an entire presidential administration, others for less than a year. They’ve used their perch at the helm of the Education Department to push a broad basket of policy priorities, from standardized testing and broader civil rights enforcement to a rollback of the federal footprint in K-12. And they’ve come from a range of backgrounds, including that of former governor, federal judiciary, state schools chief, big-city superintendent, and outspoken policy advocate.

Check out these pages for a deep look at each secretary’s tenure, challenges, and accomplishments.

The **United States secretary of education** is the head of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the president of the United States, and the federal government, on policies, programs, and activities related to all education in the United States. As a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), the secretary is sixteenth in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-2) Prior to its creation as an Executive Department, there was a non-Cabinet level position called the [United States commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commissioner_of_Education "United States Commissioner of Education") who led the [United States Office of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Education "United States Office of Education").

The current secretary of education is [Linda McMahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon"), serving in this role under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-3)

## Function

The United States secretary of education is a member of the [president's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and is the sixteenth in the [United States presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-4) This secretary deals with federal influence over [education policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy "Education policy"), and heads the United States Department of Education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-5)

The secretary is advised by the [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACIQI "NACIQI"), an advisory committee, on "matters related to accreditation and to the eligibility and certification process for institutions of higher education."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-6)

WASHINGTON, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Daniel Smith, director of the Foreign Service Institute (FSI), has been appointed acting secretary of state following Joe Biden's swearing in as President, a White House official said on Wednesday.

Smith is expected to be in the role temporarily until Biden's nominee for top diplomat, Antony Blinken, is confirmed by the U.S. Senate.

This is a **list of secretaries of state of the United States**.

## Secretaries of foreign affairs (1781–1789)

On January 10, 1780, the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") created the Department of Foreign Affairs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_secretaries_of_state#cite_note-1)

On August 10, 1781, Congress selected [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), a delegate from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), as the first secretary for foreign affairs. Livingston was unable to take office until October 20, 1781. He served until June 4, 1783, and was succeeded by [Elias Boudinot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Boudinot "Elias Boudinot"), who was succeeded by [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") on December 21, 1784, who served until March 4, 1789, when the government under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") gave way to the government under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States").

The office of secretary of foreign affairs and the Department of Foreign Affairs were reinstated by a law signed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on July 27, 1789. [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") retained the post on an interim basis, pending the return of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") from France.

## Secretaries of state

On September 15, 1789, before Jefferson could return to take the post, Washington signed into law another act which changed the name of the office from Secretary of Foreign Affairs to [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), changed the name of the department to the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), and added several domestic powers and responsibilities to both the office of secretary and the department. [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") took office as the first secretary of state on March 22, 1790.

This is a list of United States secretaries of state by time in office. This is based on the difference between dates; if counted by number of calendar days all the figures would be one greater. [Cordell Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordell_Hull "Cordell Hull") is the only person to have served as secretary of state for more than eight years. [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster") and [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") are the only secretaries of state to have ever served non-consecutive terms. [Warren Christopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Christopher "Warren Christopher") served very briefly as acting secretary of state non-consecutively with his later tenure as full-fledged secretary of state. [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") served as secretary of state for less than two weeks before becoming [ambassador to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_France "List of ambassadors of the United States to France").

response:
USA Secretaries of Commerce (including acting) from **Jan 1, 2018 through Dec 31, 2024**:

There were **no additional acting Secretaries of Commerce during 2018–2020 or 2022–2024** (the next acting secretary after Raimondo was **Jeremy Pelter**, but that began **Jan 20, 2025**, which is outside your requested range).

*The Commerce Secretary's office as it looked in the mid-20th century.*

The **United States secretary of commerce** (**SecCom**) is the head of the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to [commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce "Commerce"). The secretary reports directly to the president and is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"). The secretary is [appointed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative "Prerogative") by the president, with the [advice and consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advice_and_Consent_Clause "Advice and Consent Clause") of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of commerce is responsible for promoting American businesses and industries. The department states its mission as 'to foster, promote, and develop the foreign and domestic commerce of the United States'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-2)

Until 1913, there was one [secretary of commerce and labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce_and_Labor "United States Department of Commerce and Labor"), uniting this department with the [United States Department of Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Labor "United States Department of Labor"), which is now headed by a separate [United States secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-3)

The secretary of commerce is a [Level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-4) with an annual salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar") 250,600, as of January 2025.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-Salary-5)

The current secretary of commerce is [Howard Lutnick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Lutnick "Howard Lutnick").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-6)

## Line of succession

The line of succession for the secretary of commerce is as follows:[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-8)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Secretary_of_Commerce "Deputy Secretary of Commerce")
2. General Counsel of the Department of Commerce
3. [Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_International_Trade "Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade")
4. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Economic_Affairs "Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs")
5. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Standards_and_Technology "Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology")
6. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Oceans_and_Atmosphere "Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere") and Administrator of the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")
7. Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration
8. Chief Financial Officer of the Department of Commerce and Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Administration
9. Boulder Laboratories Site Manager, [National Institute of Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Standards_and_Technology "National Institute of Standards and Technology")

*The Commerce Secretary's office as it looked in the mid-20th century.*

The **United States secretary of commerce** (**SecCom**) is the head of the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to [commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce "Commerce"). The secretary reports directly to the president and is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"). The secretary is [appointed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative "Prerogative") by the president, with the [advice and consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advice_and_Consent_Clause "Advice and Consent Clause") of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of commerce is responsible for promoting American businesses and industries. The department states its mission as 'to foster, promote, and develop the foreign and domestic commerce of the United States'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-2)

Until 1913, there was one [secretary of commerce and labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce_and_Labor "United States Department of Commerce and Labor"), uniting this department with the [United States Department of Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Labor "United States Department of Labor"), which is now headed by a separate [United States secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-3)

The secretary of commerce is a [Level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-4) with an annual salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar") 250,600, as of January 2025.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-Salary-5)

The current secretary of commerce is [Howard Lutnick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Lutnick "Howard Lutnick").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-6)

## Line of succession

The line of succession for the secretary of commerce is as follows:[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-8)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Secretary_of_Commerce "Deputy Secretary of Commerce")
2. General Counsel of the Department of Commerce
3. [Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_International_Trade "Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade")
4. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Economic_Affairs "Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs")
5. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Standards_and_Technology "Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology")
6. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Oceans_and_Atmosphere "Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere") and Administrator of the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")
7. Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration
8. Chief Financial Officer of the Department of Commerce and Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Administration
9. Boulder Laboratories Site Manager, [National Institute of Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Standards_and_Technology "National Institute of Standards and Technology")

  **Served:** Mar 3, 2021 – Jan 20, 2025 (so she covered all of **2021–2024**)

*The Commerce Secretary's office as it looked in the mid-20th century.*

The **United States secretary of commerce** (**SecCom**) is the head of the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to [commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce "Commerce"). The secretary reports directly to the president and is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"). The secretary is [appointed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative "Prerogative") by the president, with the [advice and consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advice_and_Consent_Clause "Advice and Consent Clause") of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of commerce is responsible for promoting American businesses and industries. The department states its mission as 'to foster, promote, and develop the foreign and domestic commerce of the United States'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-2)

Until 1913, there was one [secretary of commerce and labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce_and_Labor "United States Department of Commerce and Labor"), uniting this department with the [United States Department of Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Labor "United States Department of Labor"), which is now headed by a separate [United States secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-3)

The secretary of commerce is a [Level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-4) with an annual salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar") 250,600, as of January 2025.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-Salary-5)

The current secretary of commerce is [Howard Lutnick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Lutnick "Howard Lutnick").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-6)

## Line of succession

The line of succession for the secretary of commerce is as follows:[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-8)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Secretary_of_Commerce "Deputy Secretary of Commerce")
2. General Counsel of the Department of Commerce
3. [Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_International_Trade "Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade")
4. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Economic_Affairs "Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs")
5. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Standards_and_Technology "Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology")
6. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Oceans_and_Atmosphere "Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere") and Administrator of the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")
7. Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration
8. Chief Financial Officer of the Department of Commerce and Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Administration
9. Boulder Laboratories Site Manager, [National Institute of Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Standards_and_Technology "National Institute of Standards and Technology")

The **United States secretary of energy** is the head of the [United States Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy"), a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and fifteenth in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession"). The position was created on October 1, 1977, when President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") signed the [Department of Energy Organization Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Energy_Organization_Act "Department of Energy Organization Act"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-2) establishing the department. Originally, the secretary and the department focused on energy production and regulation. Over time, the emphasis shifted to developing technology for more efficient energy sources and energy education. After the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), the department's attention also turned to radioactive waste disposal and environmental quality maintenance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-3) Former [Secretary of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Defense "United States Secretary of Defense") [James Schlesinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_R._Schlesinger "James R. Schlesinger") was the first secretary of energy. As a Republican nominated by Democratic President Jimmy Carter, Schlesinger’s appointment remains the only instance of a president choosing a member of another political party for the position. Schlesinger is also the only secretary to be dismissed from the post.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-4) [Hazel O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazel_R._O%27Leary "Hazel R. O'Leary"), [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton")’s first secretary of energy, was the first female and first African American to hold the position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-5) The first [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans "Hispanic and Latino Americans") to serve as energy secretary was Clinton’s second energy secretary, [Federico Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Pe%C3%B1a "Federico Peña"). [Spencer Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Abraham "Spencer Abraham") became the first [Arab American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Americans "Arab Americans") to hold the position on January 20, 2001, under President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"). [Steven Chu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Chu "Steven Chu"), appointed on January 20, 2009, under President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), became the first [Asian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Americans "Asian Americans") to hold the position. Chu also served as the longest-serving secretary of energy and was the first individual to join the Cabinet after having received a Nobel Prize.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-6) Former Michigan governor, [Jennifer Granholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Granholm "Jennifer Granholm"), confirmed on February 25, 2021 under President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), was the second woman to lead the Department of Energy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-7) [Chris Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Wright "Chris Wright") is the current secretary of energy under the Trump administration, confirmed on February, 4, 2025.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-8)

## Nuclear weapons

In addition to responsibilities related to generation and use of energy, the secretary is the most senior official other than the president of the United States or secretary of defense with primary responsibility for the nation's approximately 3,800 viable nuclear weapons. This arrangement is intended to maintain full civilian control over strategic weapons, except as directed by the president for specific military uses.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-9) The department of energy is responsible for the building, maintenance, and disposal of all nuclear weapons within the United States' arsenal in addition to safeguarding these weapons when they are not actively deployed in military service.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-10) Under the terms of several successive treaties, most recently New START, the United States has reduced its strategic arsenal to 1,500 deployed weapons. Consequently, many older legacy weapons systems have been dismantled or scheduled for dismantlement, with their core radioactive fuel - generally plutonium - being reprocessed into reactor-grade or space exploration fuel.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-11)

The **United States secretary of health and human services** is the head of the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services"), and serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on health matters. The secretary is a member of the [United States Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cabinet "United States Cabinet"). [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr.") is the incumbent secretary of health and human services, having held the position since February 13, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-2)

The office was formerly known as the secretary of health, education, and welfare. In 1980, the [Department of Health, Education, and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") was renamed to Department of Health and Human Services, and its education functions and [Rehabilitation Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehabilitation_Services_Administration "Rehabilitation Services Administration") were transferred to the new [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-3) [Patricia Roberts Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Roberts_Harris "Patricia Roberts Harris") headed the department before and after it was renamed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-4)

Nominations to the office are referred to the [Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor,_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions") and the [United States Senate Committee on Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance"), which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-5) before confirmation is considered by the full [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of health and human services is a [level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-6) thus earning a salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar")250,600, as of January 2025.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-Salary-7)

## Duties

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png/250px-Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare.png)

*The flag of the secretary of health, education, and welfare, the predecessor to the current office*

The duties of the secretary revolve around human conditions and concerns in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). This includes advising the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on matters of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_security "Social security"), and income security programs. The secretary strives to administer the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out approved programs and make the public aware of the objectives of the department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-8)

The [Department of Health, Education and Welfare](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "simple:United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") (HEW) was reorganized into a [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") and a [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS).

The Department of Health and Human Services oversees 11 agencies including the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA), [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") (CDC), [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH), [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") (ACF) and [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-9)

## Line of succession

The line of succession for the secretary of health and human services is as follows:[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-11)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services").
2. General Counsel of the Department of Health and Human Services
3. Assistant Secretary for Administration
4. [Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_for_Planning_and_Evaluation "Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation")
5. Administrator of the [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services")
6. [Commissioner of Food and Drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioner_of_Food_and_Drugs "Commissioner of Food and Drugs")
7. Director of the [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health")
8. Assistant Secretary for [Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families")
9. Other assistant secretaries (following in the order they took the oath of office)
  1. [Assistant Secretary for Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Assistant_Secretary_for_Health "United States Assistant Secretary for Health")
  2. [Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Assistant_Secretary_for_Preparedness_and_Response "Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response")
  3. Assistant Secretary for Legislation
  4. Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs
  5. Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources
  6. Assistant Secretary for [Aging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_on_Aging "Administration on Aging")
10. Director of the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention")
11. Director, Region 4 ([Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"))

The **United States secretary of health and human services** is the head of the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services"), and serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on health matters. The secretary is a member of the [United States Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cabinet "United States Cabinet"). [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr.") is the incumbent secretary of health and human services, having held the position since February 13, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-2)

The office was formerly known as the secretary of health, education, and welfare. In 1980, the [Department of Health, Education, and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") was renamed to Department of Health and Human Services, and its education functions and [Rehabilitation Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehabilitation_Services_Administration "Rehabilitation Services Administration") were transferred to the new [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-3) [Patricia Roberts Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Roberts_Harris "Patricia Roberts Harris") headed the department before and after it was renamed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-4)

Nominations to the office are referred to the [Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor,_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions") and the [United States Senate Committee on Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance"), which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-5) before confirmation is considered by the full [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of health and human services is a [level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-6) thus earning a salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar")250,600, as of January 2025.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-Salary-7)

## Duties

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png/250px-Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare.png)

*The flag of the secretary of health, education, and welfare, the predecessor to the current office*

The duties of the secretary revolve around human conditions and concerns in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). This includes advising the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on matters of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_security "Social security"), and income security programs. The secretary strives to administer the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out approved programs and make the public aware of the objectives of the department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-8)

The [Department of Health, Education and Welfare](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "simple:United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") (HEW) was reorganized into a [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") and a [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS).

The Department of Health and Human Services oversees 11 agencies including the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA), [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") (CDC), [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH), [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") (ACF) and [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-9)

# U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

News and analysis right to your inbox. [Click](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Email_Updates "Ballotpedia Email Updates") to get Ballotpedia’s newsletters!

From Ballotpedia

Jump to: [navigation](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#mw-navigation), [search](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#p-search)

[![New Administrative State Banner.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/7/72/New_Administrative_State_Banner.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Administrative_state "Administrative state")

The **Department of Health and Human Services** is a United States executive department established in 1979. The department was formed for "protecting the health of all Americans and providing essential human services, especially for those who are least able to help themselves."[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-hist-1)[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-mission-2)

The department oversees various agencies including, the [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://ballotpedia.org/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS), the [Food and Drug Administration](https://ballotpedia.org/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

[Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://ballotpedia.org/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr.") is the secretary of health and human services. [Click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Confirmation_process_for_Donald_Trump%27s_Cabinet_nominees,_2025-2026 "Confirmation process for Donald Trump's Cabinet nominees, 2025-2026") to learn more about his confirmation process.

## History

The department was formed as the Cabinet-level Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (HEW) in 1953 under President Dwight D. Eisenhower. In 1979 the [Department of Education](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education "U.S. Department of Education") split from HEW, and the Department of Health and Human Services was formed. Below is a list of events throughout the department's history:[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-hist-1)

- 1953: Salk polio vaccine licensed
- 1964: First Surgeon General's report on smoking and health
- 1965: Medicare and Medicaid programs created
- 1979: Department of Health and Human Services and Department of Education split from (HEW)
- 1984: National Organ Transplantation Act became law
- 1990: Human Genome Project established
- 1996: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) became law
- 1997: State Children's Health Insurance Program (SCHIP) created
- 1999: Anti-bioterrorism initiative launched
- 2003: Medicare Prescription Drug Improvement and Modernization Act enacted
- 2010: [Affordable Care Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Obamacare_overview "Obamacare overview") (ACA) became law

## Mission

According to the Department of Health and Human Services' website:[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-mission-2)

| “ | The mission of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is to enhance the health and well-being of all Americans, by providing for effective health and human services and by fostering sound, sustained advances in the sciences underlying medicine, public health, and social services.[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-3) | ” |
| --- | --- | --- |

## Leadership

The current secretary of health and human services is [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://ballotpedia.org/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr."). The secretary of health and human services advises the president on "health, welfare, and income security plans, policies, and programs of the Federal Government."[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-infoguide-4) The duties of the secretary of health and human services include:

- Overseeing a budget and employees;
- Directing department staff in carrying out the approved programs and activities of the department;
- Promoting general public understanding of the department's goals, programs, and objectives; and
- Administering these functions through 12 operating agencies, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Center for Disease Control (CDC), National Institutes of Health (NIH), and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-infoguide-4)

## Organizational chart

[Click here](https://www.hhs.gov/about/agencies/orgchart/index.html) to view the HHS organizational chart.

## Responsibilities

HHS is responsible for maintaining programs aimed at enhancing “the health and well-being of all Americans, by providing for effective health and human services and by fostering sound, sustained advances in the sciences underlying medicine, public health, and social services,” according to the department’s mission. HHS collaborates with other federal departments and agencies to pursue cross-agency collaborations on high-priority issues. HHS works with state, tribal, local, and U.S. territorial governments to administer programs, provide federal funds, and offer technical assistance for services that aim to improve the well-being of individuals, families, and communities.[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-5) [[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-6)

### Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

*See also: [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://ballotpedia.org/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services")*

The [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://ballotpedia.org/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS) oversees federal healthcare-related programs, including Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), and the health insurance exchanges created by the [Affordable Care Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act"). More than 20 different offices and divisions within the organization track the financial operations of healthcare programs or investigate efficiency improvements through new technology.[[7]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-7)

For more information about the history, structure, and responsibilities of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, **[click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services")**.

### Child Care and Development Fund

The Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) is authorized by the Child Care and Development Block Grant Act of 1990 and Section 418 of the [Social Security Act of 1935](https://ballotpedia.org/Social_Security_Act_of_1935 "Social Security Act of 1935"). CCDF “assists low-income families in obtaining child care so they can work or attend training/education. The program also improves the quality of child care, and promotes coordination among early childhood development and afterschool programs,” according to HHS. The Office of Child Care within HHS oversees the distribution of federal CCDF block grants to the states. CCDF programs are then administered by states, territories, and tribes. [[8]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-8)

CCDF contracts with providers to offer subsidized child care services to eligible families through certificates, vouchers, or grants. States have the authority to set income eligibility at or below 85 percent of the state median income and may set the maximum age for children at or below 13 years of age, or at or below 19 years of age if children have special needs, according to the Urban Institute. County governments are responsible for administering CCDF in at least eight states (Colorado, Minnesota, North Carolina, North Dakota, New York, Ohio, Virginia, and Wisconsin).

#### Role of Child Care and Development Fund in work requirements for child care subsidies

*See also: [Arguments about work requirements for public assistance programs](https://ballotpedia.org/Arguments_about_work_requirements_for_public_assistance_programs "Arguments about work requirements for public assistance programs")*

States are responsible for defining the activities that qualify a family for assistance through CCDF, such as [work requirements](https://ballotpedia.org/Arguments_about_work_requirements_for_public_assistance_programs "Arguments about work requirements for public assistance programs"), education participation, and community service. Employment is an approved activity for CCDF funding in every state and some states also approve subsidies for parents participating in education and training activities. Working, periods of job search, self-employment, attending job training or education-related activities, foster care, and subsidized guardianship are activities that meet eligibility standards for CCDF subsidies in different states. State agencies have flexibility in determining eligibility for CCDF subsidies: “Lead Agencies have flexibility to consider children’s developmental needs and specific family circumstances, such as jobs requiring split work schedules, breaks between education courses, and sleep time for parents who work multiple jobs or have nontraditional work hours.”[[9]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-11)

The **United States secretary of health and human services** is the head of the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services"), and serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on health matters. The secretary is a member of the [United States Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cabinet "United States Cabinet"). [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr.") is the incumbent secretary of health and human services, having held the position since February 13, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-2)

The office was formerly known as the secretary of health, education, and welfare. In 1980, the [Department of Health, Education, and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") was renamed to Department of Health and Human Services, and its education functions and [Rehabilitation Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehabilitation_Services_Administration "Rehabilitation Services Administration") were transferred to the new [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-3) [Patricia Roberts Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Roberts_Harris "Patricia Roberts Harris") headed the department before and after it was renamed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-4)

Nominations to the office are referred to the [Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor,_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions") and the [United States Senate Committee on Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance"), which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-5) before confirmation is considered by the full [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of health and human services is a [level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-6) thus earning a salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar")250,600, as of January 2025.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-Salary-7)

## Duties

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png/250px-Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare.png)

*The flag of the secretary of health, education, and welfare, the predecessor to the current office*

The duties of the secretary revolve around human conditions and concerns in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). This includes advising the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on matters of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_security "Social security"), and income security programs. The secretary strives to administer the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out approved programs and make the public aware of the objectives of the department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-8)

The [Department of Health, Education and Welfare](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "simple:United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") (HEW) was reorganized into a [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") and a [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS).

The Department of Health and Human Services oversees 11 agencies including the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA), [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") (CDC), [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH), [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") (ACF) and [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-9)

  3. Assistant Secretary for Legislation

# Dan Brouillette Confirmed By The U.S. Senate To Be Secretary of Energy

In a bipartisan vote of 70-15 the United States Senate confirmed Dan Brouillette to be the 15th U.S. Secretary of Energy.

[Energy.gov](https://www.energy.gov/)

December 2, 2019

![](https://www.energy.gov/themes/custom/energy_gov/img/icon-time.svg) minute read time

**WASHINGTON, D.C.** - Today, in a bipartisan vote of 70-15 the United States Senate confirmed Dan Brouillette to be the 15th U.S. Secretary of Energy. An official swearing in will take place at a later date. Prior to confirmation, Acting Secretary Brouillette served as the Deputy Secretary of Energy under Secretary Rick Perry.

“I am honored and humbled by the opportunity to serve the American people, President Trump, and DOE’s dedicated civil servants in this new role,” said **Acting Secretary Brouillette**. “I want to thank President Trump for placing his confidence in me to help advance America’s national security, energy security, and economic security through groundbreaking science, technology and innovation. I also would like to thank the Senate for its expedient review of my nomination and for the bipartisan support provided to me during the nomination hearing and tonight’s vote.

Together, we will build upon the historic progress in energy made under Secretary Perry’s leadership, making our country safer, more prosperous, and secure. I am excited for what the future holds, as our Department continues to make a lasting impact both domestically and around the world.”

The **United States secretary of energy** is the head of the [United States Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy"), a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and fifteenth in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession"). The position was created on October 1, 1977, when President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") signed the [Department of Energy Organization Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Energy_Organization_Act "Department of Energy Organization Act"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-2) establishing the department. Originally, the secretary and the department focused on energy production and regulation. Over time, the emphasis shifted to developing technology for more efficient energy sources and energy education. After the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), the department's attention also turned to radioactive waste disposal and environmental quality maintenance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-3) Former [Secretary of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Defense "United States Secretary of Defense") [James Schlesinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_R._Schlesinger "James R. Schlesinger") was the first secretary of energy. As a Republican nominated by Democratic President Jimmy Carter, Schlesinger’s appointment remains the only instance of a president choosing a member of another political party for the position. Schlesinger is also the only secretary to be dismissed from the post.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-4) [Hazel O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazel_R._O%27Leary "Hazel R. O'Leary"), [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton")’s first secretary of energy, was the first female and first African American to hold the position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-5) The first [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans "Hispanic and Latino Americans") to serve as energy secretary was Clinton’s second energy secretary, [Federico Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Pe%C3%B1a "Federico Peña"). [Spencer Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Abraham "Spencer Abraham") became the first [Arab American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Americans "Arab Americans") to hold the position on January 20, 2001, under President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"). [Steven Chu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Chu "Steven Chu"), appointed on January 20, 2009, under President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), became the first [Asian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Americans "Asian Americans") to hold the position. Chu also served as the longest-serving secretary of energy and was the first individual to join the Cabinet after having received a Nobel Prize.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-6) Former Michigan governor, [Jennifer Granholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Granholm "Jennifer Granholm"), confirmed on February 25, 2021 under President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), was the second woman to lead the Department of Energy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-7) [Chris Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Wright "Chris Wright") is the current secretary of energy under the Trump administration, confirmed on February, 4, 2025.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-8)

## Nuclear weapons

In addition to responsibilities related to generation and use of energy, the secretary is the most senior official other than the president of the United States or secretary of defense with primary responsibility for the nation's approximately 3,800 viable nuclear weapons. This arrangement is intended to maintain full civilian control over strategic weapons, except as directed by the president for specific military uses.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-9) The department of energy is responsible for the building, maintenance, and disposal of all nuclear weapons within the United States' arsenal in addition to safeguarding these weapons when they are not actively deployed in military service.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-10) Under the terms of several successive treaties, most recently New START, the United States has reduced its strategic arsenal to 1,500 deployed weapons. Consequently, many older legacy weapons systems have been dismantled or scheduled for dismantlement, with their core radioactive fuel - generally plutonium - being reprocessed into reactor-grade or space exploration fuel.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-11)

The **United States secretary of transportation** is the head of the [United States Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Transportation "United States Department of Transportation"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to transportation. The secretary is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), and is fourteenth in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-code-1)

The secretary of transportation oversees the U.S. Department of Transportation, which has over 55,000 employees and [thirteen agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Transportation#Agencies "United States Department of Transportation"), including the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration"), the [Federal Highway Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Highway_Administration "Federal Highway Administration"), the [Federal Railroad Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Railroad_Administration "Federal Railroad Administration"), and the [National Highway Traffic Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Highway_Traffic_Safety_Administration "National Highway Traffic Safety Administration").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) As of January 2021, the secretary receives an annual salary of $221,400.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-Salary-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-4)

[Sean Duffy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Duffy "Sean Duffy") has served as the 20th secretary of transportation since January 28, 2025. He was appointed by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") to serve this position, and was confirmed by the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") in a 77-22 vote.

## History

The post was created on October 15, 1966, by the Department of Transportation Act, signed into law by President [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) The department's mission is "to develop and coordinate policies that will provide an efficient and economical national transportation system, with due regard for need, the environment, and the national defense."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2)

The first secretary of transportation was [Alan S. Boyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_S._Boyd "Alan S. Boyd"), nominated to the post by Democratic president Lyndon B. Johnson. [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")'s second secretary of transportation, [Elizabeth Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Dole "Elizabeth Dole"), was the first female holder, and Mary Peters was the second. [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford")'s nominee [William Thaddeus Coleman Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Thaddeus_Coleman_Jr. "William Thaddeus Coleman Jr.") was the first African American to serve as transportation secretary, and [Federico Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Pe%C3%B1a "Federico Peña"), serving under [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton"), was the first Hispanic to hold the position, subsequently becoming the [secretary of energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Energy "Secretary of Energy"). Japanese-American [Norman Mineta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Mineta "Norman Mineta"), who had previously been the [secretary of commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Commerce "Secretary of Commerce"), is the longest-serving secretary, holding the post for over five and a half years,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) and [Andrew Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Card "Andrew Card") is the shortest-serving secretary, serving only eleven months. [Pete Buttigieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg "Pete Buttigieg") is the youngest secretary, taking office at 39 years 15 days old, overtaking [Neil Goldschmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Goldschmidt "Neil Goldschmidt") as the youngest secretary, taking office at 39 years 3 months old,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-CNBC-5) while Norman Mineta was the oldest, retiring at age 74.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTBio-6) Buttigieg is also the first openly [gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay "Gay") man to hold the position, as well as being the first openly gay Cabinet secretary, and the first to seek a full senate confirmation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-7) In April 2008, [Mary Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_E._Peters "Mary E. Peters") launched the official blog of the secretary of transportation called *The Fast Lane*.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-8) On January 23, 2009, the 16th secretary, [Ray LaHood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_LaHood "Ray LaHood"), took office, serving under the administration of Democrat [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"); he had previously been a Republican congressman from Illinois for fourteen years.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-9)

[Anthony Foxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Foxx "Anthony Foxx") was the 17th U.S. secretary of transportation from 2013 to 2017, when [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") was president. [Elaine Chao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao "Elaine Chao"), who served as the [secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor") under President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), was nominated by [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") on November 29, 2016. On January 31, 2017, the Senate confirmed her appointment by a vote of 93–6. On January 7, 2021, Chao announced her resignation following the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), effective January 11.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-10) On January 11, 2021, acting [deputy secretary of transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Transportation "United States Deputy Secretary of Transportation") [Steven G. Bradbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_G._Bradbury "Steven G. Bradbury") became acting secretary of transportation. Pete Buttigieg served as the 19th secretary of transportation during the presidency of [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").

## Line of succession

The [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_succession "Line of succession") regarding who would act as Secretary of Transportation in the event of a vacancy or incapacitation is as follows:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-14)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Secretary_of_Transportation "Deputy Secretary of Transportation")
2. [Under Secretary of Transportation for Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Transportation_for_Policy "Under Secretary of Transportation for Policy")
3. General Counsel
4. Assistant Secretary for Budget and Programs
5. Assistant Secretary for Transportation Policy
6. Assistant Secretary for Governmental Affairs
7. Assistant Secretary for Aviation and International Affairs
8. Assistant Secretary for Administration
9. Administrator of the [Federal Highway Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Highway_Administration "Federal Highway Administration")
10. Administrator of the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration")
11. Administrator of the [Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Motor_Carrier_Safety_Administration "Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration")
12. Administrator of the [Federal Railroad Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Railroad_Administration "Federal Railroad Administration")
13. Administrator of the [Federal Transit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Transit_Administration "Federal Transit Administration")
14. Administrator of the [Maritime Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Maritime_Administration "United States Maritime Administration")
15. Administrator of the [Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipeline_and_Hazardous_Materials_Safety_Administration "Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration")
16. Administrator of the [National Highway Traffic Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Highway_Traffic_Safety_Administration "National Highway Traffic Safety Administration")
17. Administrator of the [Research and Innovative Technology Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_and_Innovative_Technology_Administration "Research and Innovative Technology Administration")
18. Administrator of the [Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_St._Lawrence_Seaway_Development_Corporation "Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation")
19. Regional Administrator, Southern Region, Federal Aviation Administration
20. Director, Resource Center, Lakewood, Colorado, Federal Highway Administration
21. Regional Administrator, Northwest Mountain Region, Federal Aviation Administration

question: Can you list for me all the usa secretaries of transportation from the beginning of 2018 until the end of 2024? including short acting secretaries
response:
Here are **all U.S. Secretaries of Transportation from the beginning of 2018 through the end of 2024**, including short **acting** secretaries (i.e., anyone who served as Secretary or Acting Secretary at any point in that window):

- **Elaine L. Chao** — **Secretary of Transportation** — *Jan 31, 2017 – Jan 11, 2021*  
  (Covers **all of 2018, 2019, and 2020**, plus early 2021.)

- **Steven G. Bradbury** — **Acting Secretary of Transportation** — *Jan 12, 2021 – Jan 20, 2021*  
  (A short acting stint after Chao’s resignation.)

- **Lana Hurdle** — **Acting Secretary of Transportation** — *(served briefly in 2021; DOT history list includes her as acting between Bradbury and Buttigieg—often cited as Jan 20, 2021 – Feb 2, 2021)*

- **Pete (Peter P. Montgomery) Buttigieg** — **Secretary of Transportation** — *Feb 3, 2021 – Jan 20, 2025*  
  (Covers **2021–2024** entirely.)

Sources: U.S. DOT historical “Dates of Service: Secretaries…” list (DOT Library/History) and Buttigieg’s sworn-in date as recorded in official congressional biography materials.
